body.heading: The first week in a new place
paragraphs: Moving house is disorienting in a particular way: everything is unfamiliar at exactly the moment you have least energy for it. A short note through the new neighbour's door — your names, your house number, a welcome — lands in that week like a handrail.

Keep it brief and practical: who you are, that the kettle is available, that parcels can be left with you. New neighbours do not need a biography; they need one friendly coordinate in the new landscape.

body.heading: Follow with something edible
paragraphs: A few days later, biscuits or a small cake give the note a second chapter. Food is the oldest welcome there is, and it gives both households a reason to stand on the doorstep for five minutes, which is how acquaintances actually start.
If you missed the moving week, the note still works a month in. Late welcomes are not failed welcomes; streets are long games.

body.heading: What it starts
paragraphs: A welcomed family settles faster, borrows a ladder without dread, and keeps an eye on your house in return. The note costs ten minutes. The street it helps build lasts as long as you live on it.
If you are the new family reading this: the note works in reverse, too. A short hello from the newcomers, with names and a wave, gives the street its opening.

description: A short note and something edible in the first week can turn new neighbours from strangers into a small community.
